cards.title: Demand Gen Campaign Setup for YouTube Cold Traffic
cards.summary: Step-by-step Google Ads demand gen campaign configuration for running YouTube in-stream and Shorts as cold-traffic acquisition.
cards.use_when: Launching your first YouTube/Demand Gen cold-traffic campaign in Google Ads and you need the exact settings to configure.
steps: In Google Ads, click + > New campaign > Sales, and confirm the conversion goal is set to Purchases with a single primary conversion action.
Choose campaign type Demand Gen; name it so it's identifiable among all your campaigns. Turn OFF the product feed (source states it is never worth running on for this use case).
Bid strategy: Maximize Conversions with conversion goal = purchase. Do NOT set a target CPA yet.
Budget: minimum $100/day to start.
Location: the country you sell in (e.g. United States). Explicitly define language (e.g. English) so you don't get mis-targeted language traffic.

Devices: turn tablets OFF always. If starting from Meta only, run mobile-only at first — most conversions come from mobile in-stream/Shorts. As you scale, turn on computers and TV screens and test horizontal (16:9) ads.
Ad schedule: all day. No third-party measurement unless you're running Triple Whale (which handles this automatically).
Ad group: 'Let me choose' placements, turn OFF everything except YouTube in-stream and YouTube Shorts (turn off in-feed, Discover, Gmail, Display).
Audiences: run completely broad, no audiences — let the creative, copy and landing page do the targeting. (Source runs $8K/day broad and profitable.)
Optimized targeting: turn ON when scaling; turn OFF when only testing creative/policy compliance at low budget.
Final URL: never the homepage. Use a product page, VSSL, listicle, advertorial or quiz funnel.

Ad copy: you get up to 5 headlines at 40 characters (vs 30 in search), plus 90-character long headlines and 90-character descriptions — use the full character count. CTA: 'Shop Now'. Always turn site links off (they look bad on YouTube).
Then review and Publish.
caveats: The source's own settings ($100/day minimum, tablets off, broad targeting) are recommendations from their account experience, not platform-mandated rules.
Interface labels may change — verify the current Google Ads UI before instructing a team.

cards.title: Video Upload and Ad Group Structure for YouTube Ads
cards.summary: How to structure video ad groups and upload videos so you can test concepts and graduate winners into dedicated ad groups.
cards.use_when: Setting up the video/creative layer of a YouTube demand gen campaign and deciding how to organize ad groups.
steps: Upload your ad videos unlisted to your YouTube channel, then copy the video URL.
Paste the video URL into the ad's video box. You can add up to 5 videos per ad group.
Use the 5-slot limit to test 5 different concepts in one ad group and see which wins.
Once a winner emerges, segment it into its own ad group so you can hook-test on top of the winning control.
Structure the campaign like a CBO: one campaign containing a 'winners' ad group (clearly performing ads) and a 'testing' ad group (new/untested ads).
When a testing ad performs well in the dashboard or in Triple Whale, graduate it from testing into the winners ad group.

Placement selection by length: if the ad is under ~60 seconds, you can speed it up, shift the pitch to keep audio natural, and run it on Shorts. If it's over 60 seconds, turn Shorts off and run in-stream only.
Asset optimization: turn off the 'get shorter versions' and vertical/square auto-versions — run the creative as-is so Google doesn't cut off content.
caveats: Source runs 16:9 winners on mobile in-stream and notes it looks fine, but recommends generating a 16:9 version of winners for better CPMs as you scale.
Never run in-feed for this cold-traffic setup.

cards.title: The Six YouTube Ad KPIs and Their Ranges
cards.summary: Track six metrics — view rate, CTR, conversion rate, new customer CPA, new customer ROAS, view-through conversions — with rough good/bad ranges.
cards.use_when: Reviewing performance of a running YouTube/Demand Gen cold-traffic campaign and deciding whether to keep, pause or scale an ad.
steps: View rate (in-stream and Shorts): ~20% is really good for in-stream; ~10% is really good for Shorts. Anything above is a 'banger'.
Creative watch-depth: enable columns for 25%/50%/75%/100% watched, segmented by in-stream vs Shorts, to see how much of each video people actually watch.

CTR: above 1% is really good for in-stream (source typically sees 1.3–1.4%); 2% is 'cracked' and a massive scaler. For Shorts, 0.6%–1% is really good; closer to 1% is cracked. This measures strength of the CTA/click into your funnel.
Conversion rate: look for ~0.05% and up for both Shorts and in-stream (Google dashboard). Below that (e.g. 0.02–0.03) means work is needed on the post-click experience / landing page.

New customer CPA — the only metric that 'actually matters' in e-commerce. Track religiously in Triple Whale because Google's in-platform numbers mislead. Optimize and scale off campaign-level new customer CPA, not individual ads (ad sequencing means a converting ad may not be the one shown first).
New customer ROAS: is it above breakeven for your unit economics? A low ROAS can still mean a good CPA depending on AOV.

View-through conversions: people who watched 30+ seconds, didn't click, but later converted within the view-through window. Treat as a 'cherry on top' invisibility metric — 700 view-through conversions is effectively extra conversions baked into the campaign's total.
caveats: Ranges are the source's rough estimates from their accounts, not universal benchmarks.
New customer CPA, new customer ROAS and view-through benchmarks depend entirely on your own unit economics (COGS, shipping, LTV) and cannot be generalized.
View-through conversions exclude people converted through another Google campaign and don't count all conversions — use overall new customer CPA as the primary decision metric.

cards.title: Traffic Scaling Rules: When to Pause, Keep or Scale an Ad
cards.summary: Decision rules for pausing, holding or scaling a YouTube ad based on combined view rate, CTR, conversion and new customer CPA performance.
cards.use_when: Evaluating individual YouTube ad creatives to decide pause/continue/scale in a cold-traffic campaign.
steps: Poor metrics (poor view rate, poor CTR, no conversions, out-of-KPI new customer CPA): pause the ad immediately.
Soft metrics (okay view rate, good CTR, some conversions, KPI-level new customer CPA): keep the ad running a bit longer while searching for a stronger creative.

Strong metrics (great view rate, great CTR, new customer CPA at KPI): the source says you are 'morally obligated' to spend more money — increase the budget as fast as possible because the ad will break eventually anyway.

Scale sequence: (1) simply increase budget while still on Maximize Conversions; (2) add more creatives, always trying to beat the control; (3) hook-test the winners (in-stream has a forced 5-second view, so hooks drive view rate); (4) create a 16:9 version of winners (duplicate in Premiere/Cut, blur background and run it) to lower CPMs; (5) test new offers and CTAs to lift CTR; (6) test new conversion mechanisms to lift conversion rate; (7) only at the end, expand into in-feed with a longer, properly produced long-form video/thumbnail.
The source reports one winning ad had a Shorts CPM around $17 versus roughly $8 for its 16:9 horizontal version — this is an example, not a guaranteed result.
caveats: Scaling rules assume you already know your breakeven new customer CPA and ROAS from your unit economics — the source explicitly says it can't give a KPI threshold for these.
'Morally obligated to scale' is the presenter's strong opinion, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Segment Branded vs Non-Branded Campaigns
cards.summary: Separate branded search/shopping from cold non-branded campaigns so paid spend isn't credited with traffic organic or Meta already generated.
cards.use_when: Auditing or structuring a Google Ads account, especially for brands with existing organic or Meta-driven branded search demand.
steps: Exclude all branded terms from the main cold-traffic campaigns (e.g. Pmax and demand gen).
Build branded search and branded shopping as separate, capped campaigns rather than mixing them with prospecting.

Dig deep into how people find the store — what search terms they use — and feed that back into Google signals (custom audiences based on cold search terms, upload the customer list as an observation).
For a Meta-heavy brand, check search impression share on brand campaigns; use absolute target impression share as the bidding strategy if running brand.

If impression share is very low (the source cites cases around 14% or under 10% of page) despite cheap clicks, the brand campaign isn't achieving its goal (protecting the brand term, returning people to the funnel) — consider turning brand off entirely.
Keep brand spend capped at roughly 1%–5% of total budget if you do run it, and never let it be the primary scaling lever.
caveats: Source cites one brand where 95% of spend was on Meta with ~50% overlap before segmenting; after segmentation ~30% overlap remained and 87% of Google purchases came from previously unaware customers. This is a case result, not a promise.
Cold traffic does not equal branded conversions — turning brand off entirely is the source's opinion for Meta-heavy direct-response brands.

cards.title: Problem-Aware Creative vs Demographic Targeting on YouTube
cards.summary: Write YouTube hooks that call out the situation a problem-aware viewer is in rather than a demographic, to stay compliant and unlock broad YouTube inventory.
cards.use_when: Writing or briefing YouTube ad hooks and creative for a cold-traffic e-commerce product, especially a health/supplement/wellness offer.
steps: Write hooks around the situation/lifestyle problem the viewer is in, not the demographic. Example: for an arthritis product, don't call out 50-year-olds; talk about not being able to bend over or play with grandkids.
Aim for a 'that's me' reaction — the viewer is in an entertainment or education state, so use edutainment creatives that name their problem.
This also supports compliance because you are not linking to a specific condition or making a claim — you are describing lifestyle problems.
First 5 seconds matter most on in-stream (in-stream forces a 5-second view) — a high-quality, problem-aware hook is what carries it.

CTA should match your conversion mechanism: 'learn more' for an article/listicle/advertorial; a CTA to an offer-direct product page; a CTA to a VSSL; or a one-minute quiz ('find out which type is for you').
Make creatives highly produced, look organic and intentional, and fit the feed — avoid lazy AI-generated (e.g. ElevenLabs-style) ads.
Because YouTube inventory is massive (especially in the US), broad problem-aware creative can pull in a much wider audience than demo-targeted ads.
caveats: Source's claim that YouTube audiences are more 'sophisticated' with a higher BS detector than Meta audiences is the presenter's opinion.
Compliance claims are general guidance — always verify against current Google/YouTube ad policies for your category.

cards.title: Choose Conversion Mechanisms in Order of Proven Performance
cards.summary: The source's ordered list of YouTube conversion mechanisms — decked-out sales page first, then advertorial/quiz, then VSSL and listicles at scale.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to send YouTube cold traffic and which landing page/conversion mechanism to test for a Direct-to-Consumer product.
steps: Start with a fully decked-out product/sales page — not just a buy button. Disguise the sales process but include bundle options and the option to buy.

Next, run advertorials: information, value or story advertorials. The source prefers story advertorials because you can make the ad congruent ('I can't explain it here, click to learn more about my story').
Then try quiz funnels — source says quizzes work well on YouTube because people like interacting; it acts like a personalized consultation and disguises the sales process.
Use listicles cautiously — the source hasn't seen '5 reasons why' style lists perform as well; prefers dead sales pages and tutorial quizzes first.

VSSLs (video sales letters): only run at scale once other mechanisms are saturated. The source hasn't seen VSSLs perform as well as other options because viewers already just watched a video and are off-platform.
Match the ad CTA to the mechanism — the mechanism determines what the CTA says.
caveats: This is the source's ordered preference based on their account experience, not a universal ranking — test mechanisms against each other for your own product.
VSSL advice is explicitly contextual: it works when scaling massively and you need an additional mechanism to test.

cards.title: Set Up a New-Customer Conversion Tag
cards.summary: Install two purchase tags — a standard purchase tag plus a custom event that only fires on first order — and optimize around the new-customer event.
cards.use_when: Setting up conversion tracking for Google Ads on a store where you want to optimize for new customers rather than all purchasers.
steps: Install two tags: one traditional purchase tag, and one custom event (via the pixel or Shopify) that triggers only on a customer's first order.
Set the first-order custom event as the primary conversion action; set the standard purchase as a secondary/observation action.
Optimize campaigns around the new-customer event so Google bids toward genuine cold acquisition rather than repeat buyers.
You can build this yourself or use a tool like Blotout; the source builds it in-house for clients.
This matters because you want to be optimizing around new customers, not all purchasers, especially on cold-traffic Google campaigns.
caveats: Verify current Shopify/pixel/webhook capabilities and Google Ads conversion-action settings before building — interfaces change.
This is the source's recommended 2025 approach, not a platform requirement.

cards.title: Google Ads Budget Allocation: 80/20 for Meta-Heavy Brands
cards.summary: For a Meta-heavy direct-response brand, allocate ~80% of Google budget to Demand Gen/YouTube cold traffic and cap search/shopping/brand.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split Google Ads budget across campaign types for a brand whose acquisition is predominantly creative-led cold traffic.
steps: Focus ~80% of Google budget on demand gen (YouTube in-stream + Shorts on mobile initially), because you already have creatives and funnels and can transfer them over.
Allocate ~10–15% to search/shopping (prospecting), but only if the product has genuine category search demand.
Cap brand campaigns at ~1%–5% of budget (or turn them off entirely for Meta-heavy brands).
Skip shopping/Merchant Center entirely if the brand is gray-hat or high-AOV creative-led and likely to get banned — don't waste effort there.
Skip search entirely if your product has low search volume (e.g. a niche supplement) — you have too little volume to justify spend.
Do not use the stock agency setup (branded search, shopping/Pmax, dynamic search ads) that's copy-pasted for every brand — it doesn't account for where your traffic actually comes from.
Start on mobile until you hit ~$1K/day spend, then expand winning creatives into 16:9 and add desktop/TV placements.
caveats: The 80/20 split and the 1%/10-15% caps are the source's recommendations, not platform rules — the 80/20 principle itself is presented as a general heuristic.
As you scale, the source shifts search share up to ~20-30% for large categories with true demand.

cards.title: Demand Gen as the Cold-Traffic Engine for Meta-Heavy Brands
cards.summary: Why direct-response brands should prioritize Demand Gen/YouTube over Pmax/search for cold traffic, and when search/shopping still fits.
cards.use_when: Choosing Google campaign type for a cold-traffic e-commerce acquisition push.
steps: Identify where most of your traffic comes from — if you're predominantly Meta/cold-traffic direct response, that determines your channel choice.
Use Demand Gen (YouTube in-stream + Shorts) as the primary top-of-funnel acquisition campaign because you already have creative assets and funnels that transfer over.
Run search and shopping only when the product has inherent search demand (e.g. blood flow/pressure supplements, blue/category-specific products) or a popular branded supplement.
Avoid dynamic search ads unless you have a mass content farm with multiple product categories — the source cites a skincare one-pager with a Funnelish-based funnel that had no business running DSA.

Do not run traffic straight to a bare product page if customers need education — use advertorials, sales arguments, listicles or pre-sale pages first; product-page-direct only works for product-aware searches or when you have a live Merchant Center.
Structure the campaign so the creative + conversion mechanism carry the targeting, not detailed audience segmentation.
caveats: The source's claim that 'the creative plus mechanism is 80% of the outcome, not bidding or campaign type' is their opinion.
Search/shopping viability genuinely depends on category search volume — don't force it for low-volume products.

cards.title: PMAX for a Single Hero Product
cards.summary: Why you can run one PMAX campaign for a single hero product instead of splitting into many campaigns, and how to feed it signal.
cards.use_when: Structuring Google Ads for a store built around one hero product/SKU.
steps: If you have one hero winning product with one good funnel, you can run a single Pmax campaign across Search, Display and Shopping instead of splitting into multiple campaigns.
Never dump all products into one asset group/campaign just to scale if you have multiple products — instead consider separate bestseller and testing PMAX campaigns.
For multiple products, test the feed with a testing PMAX (e.g. feed-only on test products) and check COGS per product to confirm each is profitable independently.
Feed Google the right signals: upload the customer list as an observation, build custom audiences from cold search terms, exclude all branded terms from the main PMAX.
One clean campaign with high signal density is better than many split campaigns where Google doesn't know which channel to convert on.
Keep the setup clean — the source says 90% of the game is clean setup, exclusions and feeding Google the right data.
At sufficient spend you may get a Google rep; use that plus a tool like Microscript to dig into PMAX effectiveness (source notes PMAX is 'not the black box it used to be').
caveats: Case study results (e.g. $486K revenue on $149K spend, 1.71 new-customer ROAS on PMAX, $27.66 new customer CPA) are the source's examples, not promises.
Verify current PMAX controls and rep availability — they change over time.

cards.title: Compliance and Landing Page Prep Before Running YouTube Ads
cards.summary: Make ads, pages and product pages compliant before launching YouTube cold traffic so ads get approved and the account stays live.
cards.use_when: Preparing a health/supplement/wellness (or otherwise restricted-category) store to launch YouTube/Google ads.
steps: Audit all ads, product pages and site pages for policy compliance before spending — non-compliant pages will get ads disapproved or the Merchant Center suspended.
Make the site mobile-optimized — the source says CRO is non-negotiable and focuses 80% of traffic on YouTube mobile, so build and optimize for mobile-first.
YouTube traffic won't tolerate weak sites or scammy offers — invest in a trustworthy, high-effort, properly branded site and sales page, even if your brand isn't truly premium.
Write problem-aware copy instead of linking to a specific condition or claim, which keeps you compliant and broad.
If you can't get Merchant Center done right (proper policies, brand experience, one-of-a-kind brand), skip GMC/shopping entirely and focus on YouTube instead of fighting bans.
Disguise the sales process with education — advertorials, listicles, pre-sale pages — rather than a bare buy-button page.
caveats: Compliance requirements vary by product category and change over time — always check current Google/YouTube/Merchant Center policies.
Source's guidance is framed around banned/restricted supplement brands; not every brand needs the same caution.

cards.title: Retain YouTube Cold Traffic With Email Capture and Flows
cards.summary: Capture YouTube visitors with a popup, then run a deep welcome flow and post-purchase/replenishment sequence to extend LTV.
cards.use_when: Planning the retention and LTV layer behind a cold-traffic YouTube campaign to make acquisition economics work.
steps: Add an email popup to the landing page to capture cold visitors who don't buy immediately. Source reports a 14.7% popup conversion rate (36K unique YouTube visitors → 5.3K signups in 7 days).
Have the popup feed a welcome flow — source uses a five-email deep welcome flow that leads with a strong offer (they cite 11% discount) and drives the cold-traffic conversion.
For customers who purchase, run a post-purchase flow (thank-you + free post-purchase emails) with a replenishment/stock-up trigger — source used a 25-day wait before the replenishment email.

Because the source tracks new customer CPA as the primary metric, they say they can keep scaling while first-order profitable and rely on LTV to fix the ratio: increasing LTV is one lever if CPA can't be lowered.
Set up the retention layer as part of the acquisition plan from the start so acquired customers can be contacted for repeat purchase.
caveats: The 14.7% popup rate and 5.3K signups are case-study numbers from one brand, not benchmarks.
Retention flow specifics depend on your product's repurchase cycle; the 25-day window matched that brand's 30-day purchase cadence.

cards.title: Post-Click Landing Page Structure for YouTube Cold Traffic
cards.summary: Build a long, educational landing page with above-the-fold benefits plus stacked proof sections to convert cold YouTube traffic at ~2%.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the landing page that YouTube cold traffic is sent to and trying to lift conversion rate beyond ~0.05%.
steps: Lead with a strong above-the-fold section: benefit bullets, high-quality visuals and multiple paths to buy or get educated, not just a buy button.

Stack supporting sections in order: benefits, product details, lab results/proof, FAQs, banners, simple steps, differentiation, social proof, timelines/journeys, research and studies, community videos, founder story, a large guarantee, comparison table, more FAQs, customer reviews, additional offers/products, and a closing offer.
Use the full page as a disguise for the sales process — give people a reason to buy and to educate themselves beyond the ad.
The source's case study page converted at 2% on YouTube cold traffic (example, not a benchmark) and drove the email popup capture described above.
If your conversion rate is around 0.02–0.03%, the source attributes this to work needed on the post-click experience / landing page.
caveats: 2% on cold traffic is the source's case-study figure, not a guaranteed conversion rate.
Copying the exact section order without testing is not recommended — the source emphasizes iterating the creative and page around the audience.
